comments.text: An interesting biographical fact about the life of Maestro Zamfir:  He originally went to music conservatory with his heart dead set on learning and mastering the accordion.  But at the last minute, the accordion class closed due to lack of enrollment, and Zamfir was shoved, kicking and screaming, into the Pan Flute class.  And the rest, they say, is history...  Maestro Zamfir tells the story himself in his autobiography, Binecuvantari si Blestem, or Blessings and Curses.

comments.author: @naiman4535
comments.text: Yes - the Pan Flute, and the similar flutes in the Andes, have provided the basis of a very productive and FLUTE-ful musical relationship between Romania and Peru.  The Romanian King of the Pan Flute, Gheorghe Zamfir, has given concerts in Peru, where he was warmly and enthusiastically received.  I have heard it personally spoken from the lips of Maestro Zamfir himself that the Andean flute and folk music tradition is GREAT music, every bit on a par with his own Romanian folk music tradition.  And indeed, the Condor is the great totem power animal of all Andean musicians.  We used to finish each set of songs that we played in the Andean band with El Condor Pasa. which we jokingly called "Comida Time" or "time to eat" because after we played it, all the tourists would line up at our table to buy our CDs - and that was how we made our money.

comments.author: @naiman4535
comments.text: OMG!!!  Peru gotta be one of the wierdest, and also one of the most amazing and beautiful countries on earth.  I used to be a professional gringo pan flutist with an Andean band in San Francisco, and I took a short trip down to Peru, just to meet this lady in Lima, then go up to Cusco, and then I took the train ride from Cusco back to Macchu Picchu, and of course took photos of myself playing my pan flute there.  I sent some emails with those photos back to my Andean buddies declaring, THE CONDOR HAS LANDED! and they were impressed and amazed.  Even my old Romanian friend Marian Ionescu, who taught Pan Flute, or Nai, at a music conservatory in Targoviste Romania (Believe it or not - the original, authentic Pan Flute is NOT from South America, but is a traditional folk instrument indigenous to Romania, although similar flutes, like the Sicus, Zamponas, Antara, etc... exist in Peru and South America.  Anyway, my Romanian friend Marian Ionescu put a photo I gave him of me playing my Pan Flute / Nai at Macchu Picchu up on the wall in his office at the music conservatory.  Anyway, getting back to Peru, it is definitely a wierd and beautiful country, a total freak of Nature, where is nothing is normal or as expected.  So hurry up and get your @$$ down there!
